### Round 2
Scores are hidden, so all I know is that the three round-1 trials trained without errors. None of their results can be ranked. A brick lands one layer above the highest filled cell under its footprint, and it is correct only if the target fills exactly those cells at that layer. The starting head pools features from a trunk that has already blurred the column information through two 3x3 convolutions. Two kinds of change are worth trying: (a) give the footprint head direct access to the column features from the stem; (b) add a head that works layer by layer and learns to pick the landing layer with a softmax over height. Proposal C repeats the round-1 more-samples recipe on the skip network (proposal B). The four runs then form a 2x2 test of network and recipe, which will help when this program is rewritten.

### Round 3
Scores are hidden, so the only evidence is that all six trials trained without errors and stayed under the compute limits. I can't tell yet whether the stem skip (r2c2), the 2-epoch recipe (r1c1, r2c3), deeper trunks (r1c2) or layer-resolved encoders (r1c3, r2c1) helped. Without scores, I'm making decisions based on the task's structure. To score a placement, the policy has to work out where the brick lands (the highest build cell under its footprint) and whether the target fills exactly those cells at that layer. It also has to avoid leaving a gap under an overhang. The starting head only sees the max, min and mean of the cells under the footprint, which loses which cell is which. The per-column stem may also be too small to decode 6-layer columns. I build every proposal on the stem-skip network with the default recipe, so each one changes one thing: (1) a head that sees each footprint cell separately, (2) a deeper stem, (3) whole-board self-attention.

### Round 4
No scores are visible, so I have to rely on priors and on what the trials cover. Every trial so far trained without errors. With the default recipe, the policy changes only about 32 times per run (4,096 samples per update). That is very few, and it is probably a stronger limit than the network. Of the networks tried, the stem-skip net (r2c2) is the cheapest refinement: it adds about 8% compute and sends sharp per-column information to the footprint head, which is the most direct route to judging where a brick lands and whether it matches the target. The per-cell head (r3c1) is a natural extension of it. In this last round I keep the networks known to train and change mainly the update schedule: half as many parallel worlds (128), so the policy updates more than twice as often. I also use a longer horizon (gamma 0.97 to 0.99), so the bonus for an exact build reaches back through the whole episode and the agent learns better when to choose DONE.
